title: Design exercise: payments ledger
summary: A classic design exercise: the double-entry ledger behind a payments product, with an external provider in the loop. The reference answer keeps journal entries immutable and balanced, makes an entry atomic within one ledger shard and routes cross-ledger movement through clearing accounts, runs each payment as an orchestrated saga with idempotency at three layers, derives balances as a projection, reconciles daily against provider statements and seals history under a digest chain.

exercise.prompt: Design the ledger behind a payments product: every payment, refund, fee and payout must be recorded so that balances are always explainable, nothing is ever lost or double counted even when callers retry, and finance can prove to an auditor that the books match the money the provider actually moved.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Record money movements as double-entry journal entries; derive account balances; post a payment through an external provider (authorise, capture, refund) without duplicates; reconcile daily against provider statements; keep an immutable, verifiable history; serve balance and statement queries.

10 million payments per day; each payment produces about 6 lines across its life: two in the authorise entry (customer hold, provider clearing) and four in the capture entry (customer, merchant, fee, clearing); refunds and payouts add lines to a minority of payments and are absorbed in the rounding; 50 million accounts (customer wallets, merchant payables, provider clearing, fees, taxes); 7 years of retention (assumption shaped by typical regulation; the doc states the real requirement).
chosen for the exercise; derive the posting rate, the journal growth and the balance read load yourself

Posting is atomic and durable before acknowledgement. Same-account reads include acknowledged entries. Unresolved provider calls escalate within 10 minutes, without falsely claiming compensation succeeded. Reconciliation finishes within 6 hours of the statement; journal lines balance separately in each currency.

Fraud scoring, card networks and PCI scope (the provider holds card data), tax calculation, general ledger accounting in the finance system (this ledger feeds it), multi-currency beyond storing a currency per account.

clarifying_questions.a: Journal entries and lines are append-only; a mistake is corrected by a new reversing entry, never by an update. Balances are derived and may be recomputed.

At the ledger shard: an entry is atomic within one ledger (a set of accounts that move money among themselves). Movements between ledgers go through a clearing account as two entries linked by a saga.

Callers send an idempotency key per intent; the payment API stores the key with the outcome; retries return the stored outcome, as the Stripe write-up describes, and the provider call carries its own idempotency key.
The sum of lines on an account, held as a derived number with the sequence of the last posting it includes; two balances per account: posted and available (posted minus holds).
A merchant dashboard tolerates seconds of lag; an available-balance check before a payout must be exact, so it reads the ledger shard, not the projection.
Each account has one currency; a conversion is two entries through a currency-pair clearing account with the rate recorded on the entry.

blocks.text: The prompt's six-line estimate omits the append-only release of the memo hold. This answer uses eight lines per completed card payment so both memo and financial books balance independently. Payment volume, account count and retention remain the exercise assumptions; the revised line count changes journal storage, not provider-call or entry counts.

blocks.caption: Rates and daily volumes derived from the assumptions.
rows: two entries per payment: authorise, then capture
8 lines per payment: two memo authorisation lines, then two memo reversals and four financial settlement lines
authorise and capture; refunds, voids and payouts are a minority absorbed in the rounding
10 reads per payment (assumption): dashboards, statements and the exact checks before payouts; served from the projection except the exact checks
Little's law uses total saga lifetime: two sequential provider calls at an assumed second each, before other work and retries

blocks.caption: Sizes: the journal over the retention period and the derived balances.
rows: 5.84 TB times 7; sealed ranges move to verified cold storage
customer wallets, merchant payables, provider clearing, fees, taxes; small beside the journal
50 million accounts times about 500 bytes (assumption): posted, available and the sequence included

blocks.text: The historical latency reference lists a datacenter round trip of about 500 microseconds; it is not a measurement of this AWS path. A provider call lasting about a second is a billing and sizing assumption. Ledger commit latency, failover and end-to-end SLO feasibility need measurement under the chosen load, not an inference from that historical RTT.

Two targets shape everything else: an entry is atomic and durable before acknowledgement, and its signed lines sum to zero separately in each currency. Reconciliation repeats the per-currency check and compares provider movements. Authorisation reserves funds without counting the same hold twice.

Three systems that are often confused are kept apart. The payment orchestrator runs a saga per payment against the provider and the ledger. The ledger service accepts balanced journal entries and appends them atomically to a ledger shard. Balances and statements are projections built from the ledger's outbox events, so the hot write path never maintains them. Reconciliation compares provider statements with ledger lines on the clearing accounts, and a sealing job closes ranges of the journal under a verifiable digest.

blocks.legend: Boxes are containers; the three frames are the payment path, the derived views and the daily jobs; cylinders are stores; double brackets are logs; the provider is the external party. The ledger DB is the only source of truth: balances, statements and digests are derived from it and can be rebuilt.

blocks.text: Stripe's Ledger is described as an immutable and auditable log of events, based on double-entry bookkeeping, that validates money movement by clearing: did the fund flow complete, on time, completely. Square's Books is an immutable double-entry accounting service in which journal and book entries are append-only once stored and every entry debits one book and credits another so the accounting equation balances. Uber's LedgerStore is an immutable store with verifiable completeness and correctness guarantees that offloads older ledgers to cold storage in time-range batches. Those three are the references for the shape.

Exact reads use Aurora, while dashboards use the projection. Projector gap recovery also reads Aurora or verified archived ranges. These recovery calls are detailed in the sequence rather than additional architecture boxes. Sources: s13, s14, s20, s25, s27, s36, s52.

blocks.text: The write path through AWS, part a: accepting the payment, which the product service waits for. Edge is the internal load balancer, drawn as one lane as in the other exercises; there is no CloudFront because the callers are inside the VPC.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant P as Product svc
  participant Edge
  participant PA as Payment API
  participant DDB as DynamoDB payments
  participant SFN as Step Functions
  P->>Edge: POST with caller key
  Edge->>PA: authenticated request
  PA->>DDB: conditional PutItem
  alt caller key created
    DDB-->>PA: durable intent
    PA-)SFN: StartExecution
    PA-->>Edge: 202 payment identity
  else key already exists
    PA->>DDB: consistent GetItem
    DDB-->>PA: existing intent
    PA-->>Edge: outcome or payload conflict
  end
  Edge-->>P: response
  Note over DDB,SFN: recovery scans nonterminal intents
blocks.legend: The primary key is the authenticated caller plus its idempotency key, not a newly generated payment id. Conditional creation s15 claims that item. On conflict, an authorized strongly consistent GetItem returns the record, and the API compares a canonical payload hash before returning an outcome. StartExecution is an asynchronous hand-off, not an Express deduplication boundary. Sources: s9, s15, s35.

blocks.text: The payment API never calls the provider or the ledger: it records the intent under the caller's key and starts the saga. A retried request after a lost response hits the condition and gets the stored item back, which is the contract the Stripe write-up describes: the same key returns the same outcome.
Part b: the authorise step, asynchronous from the caller's point of view, with the provider timeout and the unknown-state branch.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 11
  participant SFN as Step Functions
  participant AD as Adapter
  participant PSP as Provider
  participant DDB as Payments
  SFN->>DDB: compare state and version
  DDB-->>SFN: current operation
  SFN->>AD: Invoke authorise
  AD->>PSP: stable authorise key
  alt confirmed authorisation
    PSP-->>AD: authorised reference
    AD-->>SFN: confirmed
    SFN->>DDB: conditional authorised state
  else unknown result
    AD-->>SFN: timeout or ambiguous result
    SFN->>DDB: conditional pending recovery
  else confirmed rejection
    AD-->>SFN: rejected
    SFN->>DDB: conditional rejected state
  end
blocks.legend: The state check is not an exclusive external-call lock: duplicate executions may repeat the same stable provider operation key. They cannot advance a different operation until its predecessor and ledger step are recorded. Conditional predecessor/version updates prevent regression, and terminal outcomes are protected. Unknown outcomes are queried or retried with the same operation key, never treated as rejection. Sources: Retry/Catch s10, saga pattern s8, NAT s26, Express s9.

blocks.text: Express StartExecution is not idempotent. This design permits duplicate executions but conditions every state update on the expected predecessor and version; terminal states cannot regress. Provider operations use stable operation-specific keys. Only a confirmed rejection permits compensation; an unknown result remains pending while recovery queries or retries that same operation. A durable index of every nonterminal intent lets recovery find API deaths and executions killed at the five-minute limit even if no needs_recovery write happened. Recovery replays incomplete idempotent steps and escalates unresolved intents at ten minutes without declaring them compensated.
Part c: posting an entry, the step both the authorise and the capture branches share.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 22
  participant SFN as Step Functions
  participant LS as Ledger svc
  participant LD as Aurora writer
  SFN->>LS: post entry with step key
  LS->>LD: BEGIN and lock ledger head
  alt new valid balanced entry
    LS->>LD: lines, holds, sequence, outbox
    LS->>LD: COMMIT
    LD-->>LS: durable sequence
  else duplicate step key
    LD-->>LS: existing entry and sequence
  else failure or invalid entry
    LD-->>LS: rollback or unknown commit
  end
  LS-->>SFN: result or retry same key
blocks.legend: One transaction holds the entry, its lines, the per-ledger sequence and the outbox row, so nothing is published that was not committed. RDS Proxy pools the function's connections in front of the writer s13; a writer failover promotes a replica and service is typically restored in under a minute s11; the cluster volume is copied across three Availability Zones s12.

blocks.text: Part d: capture, the stored outcome, and the compensation when the capture is rejected after the authorise.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 30
  participant SFN as Step Functions
  participant AD as Adapter
  participant PSP as Provider
  participant LS as Ledger svc
  participant DDB as Payments
  SFN->>AD: capture with stable key
  AD->>PSP: capture
  alt confirmed capture
    PSP-->>AD: captured
    AD-->>SFN: confirmed
    SFN->>LS: post capture with step key
    LS-->>SFN: durable entry
    SFN->>DDB: conditional captured state
  else confirmed rejection
    AD-->>SFN: rejected
    SFN->>AD: confirm void with stable key
    AD-->>SFN: confirmed void or unknown
    opt void confirmed
      SFN->>LS: reverse reservation
      SFN->>DDB: conditional compensated
    end
  else unknown result
    AD-->>SFN: unknown
    SFN->>DDB: conditional pending recovery
  end
blocks.legend: Capture and compensation are mutually exclusive paths. An unknown capture is resolved before any void or reversal. Only a confirmed void allows reservation release. Retries use immutable step keys and conditional predecessor/version transitions; terminal captured or compensated states cannot regress. A worker resolves overdue nonterminal intents even if the execution dies before recording recovery. Sources: s10 and s8.

The internal load balancer has no public address. Public NAT gateways provide outbound provider access; they do not accept unsolicited inbound connections.

blocks.text: The read path through AWS, part a: the derived path from the committed entry to the projected balance, which no caller waits for.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant LD as Aurora
  participant RL as Outbox relay
  participant K as Kinesis stream
  participant BP as Projector
  participant BAL as DynamoDB balances
  RL->>LD: read pending entries
  LD-->>RL: ledger sequences
  RL->>K: PutRecords
  K-->>RL: per-record outcomes
  RL->>LD: mark only successes sent
  K-)BP: entries may be reordered
  BP->>BAL: read ledger watermark
  BAL-->>BP: contiguous watermark
  alt next sequence
    BP->>BAL: atomic deltas and watermark
  else gap or expired log
    BP->>LD: read missing journal range
    LD-->>BP: contiguous entries
    BP->>BAL: apply each next sequence
  end
blocks.legend: PutRecords can partially fail and reorder records. The relay retries only failed records and never marks an unacknowledged record sent. This application protocol, not partition-key ordering, supplies correctness: one logical projector per ledger conditionally advances a ledger watermark by exactly one, transactionally with every affected balance and hold delta. Duplicates at or below the watermark are skipped. Gaps are filled from the journal or verified archive, never skipped. Limit the entry's affected items to the DynamoDB transaction limit. Kinesis is short-lived delivery, not the rebuild source. Sources: s14, s15, s18, s20.

blocks.text: Part b: a balance read, from the projection, and the exact check before a payout.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 13
  participant R as Dashboard
  participant Edge
  participant PA as Payment API
  participant BAL as DynamoDB balances
  participant LD as Aurora
  R->>Edge: GET balance
  Edge->>PA: authenticated request
  alt exact read
    PA->>LD: consistent snapshot and holds
    alt valid snapshot and writer
      LD-->>PA: exact balance and watermark
    else unavailable or corrupt
      LD-->>PA: fail closed
    end
  else dashboard
    PA->>BAL: GetItem
    BAL-->>PA: projected balance and age
  end
  PA-->>Edge: balance or unavailable
  Edge-->>R: response
  Note over PA,LD: spending requires a transaction
blocks.legend: Exact reads do not trust the dashboard projection. They use a validated ledger snapshot plus contiguous journal and hold transitions in one database snapshot, or fail closed. Spending separately locks the ledger head and reserves or posts atomically. A corrupted snapshot is rebuilt from authoritative journal/archive before use. Sources: gateway endpoint s35, Aurora failover s11 and RDS Proxy s13.

blocks.text: Part c: the daily jobs, started by EventBridge Scheduler: reconciliation against the provider's statement and the sealing of yesterday's range.

  participant RC as Reconciliation
  participant LD as Aurora
  participant SL as Sealing

    PSP-)S3: daily statement
    RC->>S3: GetObject
    S3-->>RC: statement

blocks.legend: Sources: cron schedules in EventBridge Scheduler s27; the S3 gateway endpoint s36; Object Lock's compliance mode, under which no user can overwrite or delete the digest before its retention date s25; sealing and cold storage in time-range batches at Uber s3.

blocks.text: This design's digest chain and Object Lock copy detect later journal tampering; they do not prevent database edits. Uber supports sealing and time-range cold storage, not this exact digest protocol. An auditor verifies the retained chain against the journal and archive. Reconciliation cases and digests are metadata writes, not edits to journal lines.

blocks.caption: The ledger store: Aurora PostgreSQL, DynamoDB with transactions, RDS for PostgreSQL, or Aurora DSQL.

rows.pick_when: an entry is several rows that must commit together with an invariant checked inside the transaction, the hot path needs range scans by sequence, and reconciliation and audit need SQL
rows.avoid_when: every access is a key lookup at a rate that would leave always-on instances idle, or the team cannot shard by a natural key
rows.example: For this design: chosen, one cluster per ledger shard. An entry is one transaction over the entry row, its lines, the per-ledger sequence and the outbox row, with the sum-to-zero check inside it; a writer in one zone, a reader in another, the cluster volume in three zones; failover typically under a minute.

rows.pick_when: entries are small and key-shaped, the invariants can be expressed as item conditions, and nobody wants instances or capacity planning
rows.avoid_when: an invariant must be computed over the rows inside the transaction, the design needs a dense per-ledger sequence, or reconciliation needs ad hoc queries
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for the journal. Transactional key access is viable, but database-side balanced-entry validation and reconciliation range queries favor SQL. DynamoDB holds the key-shaped derived balances with conditional transactional watermark advancement.

rows.pick_when: managed PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ standby replication and failover fits the workload, or required extensions favor RDS
rows.avoid_when: measurement shows Aurora's storage or read-scaling model better meets this workload's requirements
rows.example: For this design: Aurora is a workload choice for its cluster storage and read scaling, not because RDS lacks managed replication or promotion. RDS Multi-AZ remains a valid alternative requiring the same recovery testing.

rows.pick_when: the product needs an active-active, multi-Region relational store with strong consistency and no instances to manage
rows.avoid_when: the entry transaction has not been measured on its concurrency model, or the drivers and schema rely on PostgreSQL features it does not provide
rows.example: For this design: not yet. The decision guide describes it as serverless distributed SQL with active-active multi-Region replication and strong consistency, which is the shape a multi-Region ledger platform at 10x would evaluate, after measuring the entry transaction on it.

blocks.caption: The ledger events: Kinesis Data Streams, SQS, EventBridge, or Amazon MSK.

rows.pick_when: consumers need per-key ordering, replay of retained history, or several independent readers of the same stream; the producer can batch records
rows.avoid_when: the volume is tiny, nobody replays, and one consumer with at-least-once delivery is all that is needed
rows.example: For this design: chosen for asynchronous delivery, not as the authority for history. Partition keys select shards but PutRecords can reorder. The projector recovers gaps from the journal or verified archive. The priced model has one consumer; extra exports need separate read charges.

rows.pick_when: one consumer, idempotent work, no ordering needed, and the simplest possible hand-off
rows.avoid_when: consumers need order, replay, or several of them need every event
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. The projector depends on sequence order per ledger and on replay; a standard queue offers neither, and the FIFO variant orders but does not retain history for a rebuild.

rows.pick_when: events of many shapes are routed by rules to many targets, across accounts, and the routing matters more than throughput or order
rows.avoid_when: one high-volume stream of identical events feeds one or two consumers in order
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Ledger events have one shape and ordered consumers; rule-based routing buys nothing here.

rows.pick_when: the team already runs Kafka clients and tooling, needs its ecosystem, or the throughput and retention make broker-level control worth the operations
rows.avoid_when: about 20 GB of events a day with two consumers, where a managed stream needs no brokers to size or patch
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. The stream carries about 20 GB a day; Kinesis on-demand scales that without shards to manage, and the Kafka ecosystem is not needed.

blocks.caption: The saga: Step Functions Standard, Step Functions Express, an orchestrator service on Fargate, or EKS.

rows.pick_when: executions are long (up to a year), steps are not idempotent so exactly-once matters, and the volume is thousands of executions a day
rows.avoid_when: millions of short executions a day, because the bill is per state transition
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. At 10 million payments a day the transitions would cost about $60,000 a month, more than the rest of the design together, and the steps are already idempotent, so exactly-once buys nothing.

rows.pick_when: high-volume, short workflows whose steps are idempotent, so at-least-once execution is safe, billed per request and duration
rows.avoid_when: an execution must outlive five minutes, or must never run twice
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The happy path is two provider calls and two ledger writes in a few seconds; every step carries its own key, so a re-run is a no-op; a step that outlives its retries hands the payment to the recovery worker, which re-drives it and escalates at ten minutes.

rows.option: An orchestrator service on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate
rows.pick_when: the saga must hold connections, run for hours, or its volume makes a per-execution bill cost more than a few always-on tasks
rows.avoid_when: the team would reimplement timeouts, retries, history and a scheduler that the managed workflow already provides
rows.example: For this design: the alternative at 10x. The recovery worker already is such a service; moving the whole saga into it would trade the Express bill and the Lambda time spent waiting on the provider for a few tasks and the team's own state machine.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes and wants the saga's services inside it, with its ecosystem and portability
rows.avoid_when: a handful of stateless functions and services with no Kubernetes estate; the cluster fee, the upgrade cadence and the SRE time buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing here needs the Kubernetes API, and a cluster brings three major releases a year to track.

blocks.text: Within that choice, the payment API, the relay, the recovery worker and the two jobs run as ECS on Fargate tasks (steady internal traffic, held connections, scheduled batches), and the two saga participants are Lambda functions because Step Functions invokes them from Task states with Retry and Catch; the decision guide's rule of thumb holds, Lambda for event-shaped bursts and Fargate for sustained work. The adapter's time waiting on the provider is the line in the cost table that a long-running adapter would remove.

The cache fork does not apply to this design: nothing is cached. The balance projection is a derived view, not a cache, and the exact check deliberately reads the ledger; a cache in front of either would reintroduce the staleness the exact path exists to remove.

rows: {amount, currency, from, to, intent} with an Idempotency-Key header

{lines[], kind, reference} with an idempotency key
{entry_id, sequence}, or 422 if the lines do not balance

built from the same event stream as balances

blocks.text: Amounts are integers in minor units and every entry carries its currency, so a balance is a sum, never a rounding. The idempotency key on the payment API is the caller's intent; the key on the ledger API is the saga step, which is what lets a replayed saga post the same entry twice and get the same sequence back.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: A card payment from a customer to a merchant, with the provider in the loop. The saga is orchestrated (one coordinator per payment) rather than choreographed, so the state of every payment is in one place; the step numbers run on across the five parts.
Part a: the payment API accepts the request and answers before any provider call.

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant P as Product service participant PA as Payment API participant O as Orchestrator P->>PA: POST /payments, Idempotency-Key alt the key is known PA-->>P: the stored outcome else a new key PA->>PA: Payment created PA-)O: start the saga PA-->>P: {payment_id, created} end Note over P,O: one coordinator per payment,
its state is in one place
blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed; the open arrow is the hand-off to the saga. A known key returns the stored outcome, which is the idempotency contract Stripe's API describes s5.

blocks.text: Part b: authorise at the provider, then post the authorise entry.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 6
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant AD as Adapter
  participant PSP as Provider
  participant LS as Ledger svc
  participant LD as Ledger DB

  AD->>PSP: authorise

    PSP-->>AD: authorised
    AD-->>O: confirmed

blocks.legend: A provider memo hold is not a debit to a funded wallet. It records external authorisation in a separate memo book, excluded from financial posted and available balances. Unknown provider outcomes remain unresolved until queried or retried with the same operation key. Shopify supports timeout and circuit-breaker choices s6, not this specific accounting model.

blocks.text: Part c: capture at the provider, post the capture entry, and the compensation when a step fails after its predecessor succeeded.

  participant LD as Ledger DB
  O->>AD: capture with operation key
  AD->>PSP: capture

    PSP-->>AD: captured
    AD-->>O: confirmed

    LD-->>LS: sequence
    LS-->>O: durable entry
  else confirmed rejection

    AD-->>O: confirmed or unknown

    end

blocks.legend: Capture releases the memo hold and posts financial settlement in one entry. Rejection leads to a memo reversal only after a confirmed provider void. Unknown capture results are resolved before compensation. The worked postings below are this design's accounting convention, not a claim about Square's exact schema.

blocks.legend: The relay records successful publication per record and retries failures. Projection applies the next ledger sequence only, atomically with all affected financial balances and local reservations. Provider memo lines never reduce available funds. Gaps come from the authoritative journal/archive; a missing or corrupt range stops advancement.

blocks.text: Part e: the daily jobs, reconciliation against the provider's statement and the sealing of the previous day's range.

  participant SL as Sealing job

blocks.legend: Every mismatch (in the ledger but not at the provider, the reverse, or an amount difference) becomes a case with an owner; corrections are adjustment entries, never edits. Reconciliation against the partner's records is Shopify's seventh rule s6; sealing and offloading sealed ranges in time-range batches is what Uber describes for LedgerStore s3.

blocks.text: The caller's scoped key identifies intent, each provider operation has a stable key derived from payment identity and operation, and each ledger step has its own key. Duplicate executions may run, so predecessor/version conditions guard transitions and terminal states never regress. Recovery examines every overdue nonterminal intent, queries unknown provider outcomes and resumes only the incomplete step. It never interprets a timeout as permission to reverse a captured payment.

The write path is a single transaction per entry on one shard, which is what makes atomicity cheap: all accounts of an entry live in the same ledger. The cost of that rule is cross-ledger movement, which becomes two entries through a clearing account (debit the source ledger's clearing account, credit the destination ledger's), linked by the saga and reconciled by the rule that clearing accounts net to zero across ledgers.

blocks.title: The serialization boundary and safe spending
items: A captured payment writes gross and fee lines to the merchant payable account.
A tenth of peak payments gives about 232 lines per second there under this worked posting model; this is an assumption, not a measured locking bottleneck.
The dense per-ledger sequence already serializes updates to the ledger head. Benchmark that critical section before selecting shard count.
Entry, lines, hold transitions, sequence and outbox are written together. Dashboard balances remain a separate, rebuildable projection.

For spending, lock the ledger head and read a consistent journal-derived balance plus active holds. Atomically reject insufficient funds or reserve/post, so concurrent payouts cannot spend the same balance.

An exact read may use only a validated, immutable ledger snapshot with a contiguous watermark plus all later lines and hold transitions. If integrity fails, stop spending and rebuild from the journal or verified archive, not from the corrupted projection.

blocks.text: Idempotency has three layers and each needs its own key: the caller to the payment API (intent), the orchestrator to the provider (payment id), and the orchestrator to the ledger (saga step id), so a crash between any two steps is recoverable by replaying the saga from its stored step. Uber's write-up on money movement at scale describes the same insistence: orders are immutable, unique identifiers make processing idempotent, and the platform reconciles itself.

Reconciliation is the last line and the most important one: it catches what idempotency cannot (a provider that charged without telling us, a bug that posted the wrong amount), so it is a product feature with cases, owners and ageing, not a script. Shopify's rule is the same: make sure our records are consistent with those of our financial partners.
Each row names the failure, what happens to the money, and the mitigation.

blocks.text: At that scale the ledger is a platform for many products, and reconciliation becomes a service with per-provider adapters and a cases workflow. A migration from a legacy ledger is the hard project: dual posting into old and new, a daily side-by-side reconciliation of balances, a cutover criterion of zero differences for a set period, and reversing entries to repair, never edits. The question the staff engineer asks is which products need a ledger at all and which only need a provider's statement.

Teaching journal volumes use decimal bytes. Billing allowances round upward into AWS GB units rather than equating decimal TB with binary storage. Journal storage is budgeted separately from statements, and stream bytes include metadata and record rounding. The month uses 30 request-days and 730 running hours.

Authorise advances only the watermark. Capture updates three financial accounts and the watermark. Five transactional item writes consume ten write units per payment.
Ten eventual dashboard reads and three strong reads per payment: two projector watermark reads plus one saga-state read. Every read item is below four KiB.
25 billed GB for balances plus one billed GB watermark allowance. No projection indexes.
Two jobs, each four vCPUs and eight GB, run one hour daily.
Scale every Fargate task and daily job count tenfold. This is an explicit fleet assumption, not a benchmark.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: distinguish memo holds from financial settlement, state per-currency balance, derive the revised eight-line lifecycle and its journal growth, and use total saga lifetime for concurrency.

0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Ledger, Account, JournalEntry, Line with the sum-to-zero rule, Hold, Balance as a projection, Payment with its saga step, SealedRange; amounts as integers in minor units.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: orchestrator, provider adapter, ledger service and shards, outbox to events, balance projector, reconciliation, sealing. Say which system is the source of truth and which are derived.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: the saga with its three idempotency layers and compensations (what happens when the provider times out after authorising), then the ledger write path (atomic per shard, clearing accounts, hot accounts and projected balances, the exact balance check).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x platform (ledgers per product, sealing to cold storage, the legacy migration), and the L3 sentence: idempotency prevents most duplicates and reconciliation finds the rest; a ledger without reconciliation is a database with opinions.

Context and scope: The products that move money today, the providers, the finance system that consumes the books, the audit or incident that motivates the ledger, and the retention regulation that applies.
Goals and non-goals: Atomic, durable, idempotent posting; explainable balances; daily reconciliation; verifiable history; no fraud scoring, no card data, no general ledger accounting.
Design: This answer fills it: the data model with the sum-to-zero rule, the saga, the shard atomicity rule, projections, reconciliation and sealing.
Alternatives considered: Balance columns on the write path, choreographed sagas, global transactions, in-place corrections, trusting the database for completeness, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Security (who may post, who may adjust, four-eyes on adjustments, audit log of operator actions), privacy (no card data; account references only), observability (saga age, compensation rate, reconciliation open cases by age, projection lag), cost (storage over 7 years, provider fees are not this system's cost but its data), rollout with dual posting and a reconciliation period.

Review questions the doc must answer: What the system does when the provider authorised but the response was lost, and how a wrong posting discovered a month later is corrected without touching history.
